paras: The lynching of Nick Thompson took place near Amory, Mississippi, on September 1, 1910, when a mob reported at about 2,000 hanged Thompson, a Black man accused of assaulting a 17-year-old white girl, to a telegraph pole. Three days earlier, crowds had threatened to storm the jail to lynch another suspect, who was released as not the man sought. Wire reports stressing the crowd's size ran nationally, and a local weekly used the case to campaign for Vardaman.

According to an Associated Press dispatch, the 17-year-old daughter of William Jackson, a planter, was attacked late on Saturday, August 27, in a thicket on her way home from a neighboring plantation. The Aberdeen Weekly named her as Jennie Jackson of Jackson Crossing and said a man hidden in the underbrush attacked her; dogs from New Albany were put on his trail. Her condition was reported as serious, and the Hattiesburg News called her recovery doubtful.

On August 29 a sheriff's posse captured a Black man in a barn near the scene and took him to jail under strong guard. That night excited crowds marched through Amory threatening to storm the jail, and a midnight telegram relayed through Memphis reported a mob forming to lynch him. A Starkville dispatch instead described a thousand men around Stockton's stables, "clamoring for the life of a negro concealed in a stall," as officers and "the best citizens" tried to stay them.

On August 30 the prisoner was released after proving he was not the man wanted, and three other arrested Black men were brought for the young woman to identify. A later account put those arrested besides Thompson at six, all freed on alibis, and said only "cooler heads" had prevented a lynching at the first arrests.

On September 1, according to the Associated Press, Jennie Jackson identified Nick Thompson, and as soon as this became known a mob formed, took him to the scene of the crime, and hanged him to a telegraph pole before dispersing. A United Press account said "two thousand citizens, friends of Jackson" dragged him from the jail at night, lowered him after a minute to demand a confession, and hoisted him again until he died.
The reports end with the mob dispersing; none mentions an inquest, arrests of mob members, or a prosecution.

The first wave of coverage, on August 30 and 31, carried Associated Press dispatches under headlines such as "Mob Needs Only Leader" and "Mob Forms to Lynch," with the town garbled as "Amoy" or "Amery." The Hattiesburg News called the assault "alleged" but predicted the man's life would be "forfeited at the stake," while the release drew only short items such as "Negro Is Released."

From September 2 the lynching report ran from Washington and Newport News to Texas, Kentucky, Georgia and New Jersey, under headlines such as "Two Thousand at a Lynching" and "Girl Identifies Negro; Strung Up by Mob." The wire text called Thompson "accused," but headlines often treated the charge as proven, from Montgomery's "Lynched Negro Who Assaulted White Girl" to Americus's "Fiend is Strung up There for Usual Crime."

Writing before any identification, the Aberdeen Weekly called the attacker "the fiend," predicted he would be "sent by the rope route to death," and argued that the "Vardaman doctrine" on the race question was not "fictitious." All the accounts located were in white papers; no Black newspaper report of the case appears among them.

The Associated Press said Thompson was taken to the scene in the afternoon, while the United Press said he was dragged from the jail at night. The young woman's age was 17 in most reports, including the local weekly, 16 in the release item, and "seven" in the United Press text, probably a garbling. Early accounts placed the first suspect in the jail or, per Starkville, in Stockton's stables, and the Memphis telegram called the charge attempted assault.

reader.title: Lynching of Nick Thompson
bases: Mobs threatened to storm the jail for a first suspect on Aug 29 (A1, A3, A6), and on Sept 1 a mob reported at 2,000 hanged Nick Thompson, accused of the same assault (A10, A13).

Thompson was hanged to a telegraph pole by a mob of about 2,000 with no legal process (A10, A13), after being identified as the man accused of assaulting a white girl, a pretext of punishing a crime (A10, A12).

Independent Associated Press and United Press dispatches agree that Thompson was hanged by a mob of about 2,000 at Amory (A10, A13), and the earlier mob threats appear in separate AP and Starkville dispatches and the local Aberdeen Weekly (A1, A6, A14).

accounts.gist: Crowds marched the streets threatening to storm the county jail, where a suspect captured by a sheriff's posse was held under strong guard; they waited only for a leader.

accounts.label: Starkville dispatch
accounts.gist: A thousand men surrounded Stockton's stables clamoring for a man concealed in a stall, and his death at the stake seemed probable; officers and leading citizens could not stay them.

accounts.label: Local weekly (Aberdeen)
accounts.gist: A man hidden in underbrush assaulted Jennie Jackson; dogs from New Albany were put on his trail and several Black men were held, none yet identified.

accounts.label: Associated Press, Sept 1
accounts.gist: After Jennie Jackson identified Thompson, a mob of about 2,000 took him to the scene in the afternoon, hanged him to a telegraph pole, and dispersed.

accounts.label: United Press
accounts.gist: About 2,000 'friends of Jackson' dragged Thompson from the jail at night, lowered him after a minute to demand a confession, and hanged him again until dead when he refused.

framing.detail: Brief AP Memphis items ('Mob Forms to Lynch') ran in Oklahoma, California and Florida papers, garbling the town as 'Amery'.
The Hattiesburg News headline 'Amory Mob Clamors for Life of a Negro' called the assault 'alleged' while forecasting death 'at the stake'.
AP lynching text said 'accused' and 'alleged victim', but the Montgomery headline 'Lynched Negro Who Assaulted White Girl' stated the charge as fact.
The Aberdeen Weekly called the attacker 'the fiend', predicted the 'rope route to death', and used the case to promote the 'Vardaman doctrine'.
The Americus Times-Recorder headlined 'Fiend is Strung up There for Usual Crime'.
